py-hello: A program is a list of instructions that the computer follows, one after the other, from the top line to the bottom line. In this first lesson you will make Python show text on the screen, which is how every program talks back to you. ### print shows something on the screen print is a function: a ready-made command that does a job for you. To use it, you write its name followed by round brackets, called parentheses: ( ). Whatever you put inside the parentheses is what gets shown in the output area. ~~~python print("Good morning") print("Python is ready") ~~~ - Line 1: print receives the text Good morning and writes it as one line of output. - Line 2: Python moves to the next line and prints Python is ready on a new line. Each print starts a new line. ### Text needs quotes: strings A piece of text in Python is called a string. You must wrap it in quotes so Python knows where the text starts and stops. Double quotes "..." and single quotes '...' both work, as long as the opening and closing quotes match. The quotes themselves are not printed. Everything between them is printed exactly as written: spaces, commas, capital letters and punctuation included. ~~~python print("Hello, friend!") print('Single quotes work too.') print(" spaces are kept ") ~~~ - Line 1: prints Hello, friend!. The comma and the exclamation mark are part of the text, so they appear. - Line 2: the same idea with single quotes. The output shows no quotes at all. - Line 3: the spaces inside the quotes are printed too, because they are part of the string. ### Numbers do not need quotes Numbers are written as they are, with no quotes. Python can then do maths with them. The + sign adds, - subtracts. ~~~python print(2 + 3) print("2 + 3") print(10 - 4) ~~~ - Line 1: Python first calculates 2 + 3, gets 5, then prints 5. - Line 2: this time the characters are inside quotes, so it is just text. Python prints 2 + 3 without calculating anything. - Line 3: Python calculates 10 - 4 and prints 6. ### Several things in one print You can give print several values separated by commas. It prints them on one line with a single space between each. ~~~python print("Total:", 5 + 5) print("Apples", "and", "pears") ~~~ - Line 1: two values. The text Total:, then the result of 5 + 5. The output is Total: 10. - Line 2: three strings, joined with spaces: Apples and pears. ### Comments are notes for humans A line that starts with # (the hash sign) is a comment. Python skips it completely. You can also put a comment at the end of a line: everything after the # is ignored. Comments are for explaining your code to people. ~~~python # This line is ignored by Python print("Only this is shown") # a note after the code ~~~ - Line 1: a comment. Nothing happens. - Line 2: prints Only this is shown. The part after # is ignored. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting a quote: print("Hello) stops with a SyntaxError, because Python cannot find where the text ends. - Writing Print with a capital P. Python is case sensitive: only print exists. - Forgetting the parentheses: print "Hi" does not work in Python 3. - Typing the text slightly differently from what is asked. A missing comma or a lowercase letter counts as a different string. ~~~text print("Hello) SyntaxError: unterminated string literal ~~~ ### Recap - A program runs from top to bottom, one line at a time. - print(...) shows what is inside the parentheses, then moves to a new line. - Text is a string and goes inside matching quotes. Numbers have no quotes. - Commas inside print separate several values, shown with a space between them. - # starts a comment that Python ignores.
py-vars: Programs need to remember things: a customer's name, a price, whether an order is paid. A variable is how Python remembers a value so you can use it later by name. ### Creating a variable with = A variable is a name that points at a value. You create one with the = sign. In Python, = does not mean "is equal to" like in maths. It means "store the value on the right under the name on the left". This is called an assignment. ~~~python name = "Ada" print(name) print("name") ~~~ - Line 1: Python creates a variable called name and stores the string "Ada" in it. - Line 2: name has no quotes, so Python looks up the variable and prints its value: Ada. - Line 3: "name" has quotes, so it is just the text name. Quotes make the difference. ### Changing a variable A variable can be given a new value at any time. The old value is replaced. You can also use a variable to compute a new value. ~~~python score = 10 print(score) score = 25 print(score) bonus = score + 5 print(bonus) ~~~ - Line 1: score holds 10. - Line 2: prints 10. - Line 3: score now holds 25. The 10 is forgotten. - Line 4: prints 25. - Line 5: Python reads score (25), adds 5, and stores 30 in a new variable bonus. - Line 6: prints 30. ### The four basic types Every value has a type, which says what kind of value it is. These four are the ones you will use all the time: - str (string): text, always in quotes, like "Lyon". - int (integer): a whole number with no decimal point, like 42 or -7. Never write spaces or commas inside it: one million is 1000000. - float: a number with a decimal point, like 3.5. Python uses a dot, not a comma. - bool (boolean): either True or False. They start with a capital letter and have no quotes. Use them for yes or no facts. ~~~python city = "Paris" rooms = 4 price = 129.99 has_pool = False print(city, rooms, price, has_pool) ~~~ - Line 1: city holds a string. - Line 2: rooms holds an int. - Line 3: price holds a float. - Line 4: has_pool holds the bool False. - Line 5: prints all four values on one line: Paris 4 129.99 False. ### Asking Python for the type You never have to announce the type: Python works it out from the value. The type() function tells you which type a value has. You can put one function inside another: print(type(x)) first asks for the type of x, then prints the answer. ~~~python rooms = 4 price = 129.99 print(type(rooms)) print(type(price)) print(type("4")) print(type(True)) ~~~ - Lines 1 and 2: create two variables. - Line 3: type(rooms) gives the int type, and print shows it as <class 'int'>. - Line 4: prints <class 'float'> because 129.99 has a decimal point. - Line 5: "4" is in quotes, so it is a string, not a number: <class 'str'>. - Line 6: prints <class 'bool'>. ### Naming rules Variable names use lowercase words joined by underscores, like is_capital or total_price. A name can contain letters, digits and underscores, but it cannot start with a digit and cannot contain spaces. Names are case sensitive: City and city are two different variables. ### Common mistakes - Writing false or "False". The bool is False, capital F, no quotes. With quotes it is just text. - Putting a number in quotes: "522000" is a string, not an int. - Writing 522,000 or 522 000. Python does not accept separators inside a number like this. - Using a variable before creating it, which stops the program with a NameError. ### Recap - name = value stores a value under a name. A later assignment replaces it. - Without quotes, a name means "the value of this variable". With quotes, it is just text. - The basic types are str, int, float and bool. - type(value) tells you the type, and print(type(value)) shows it.
py-math: Python is an excellent calculator. Prices, totals, averages and time conversions are all simple arithmetic, and this lesson gives you every operator you need for them. ### The basic operators An operator is a symbol that does a calculation with the values on each side of it. - + adds, - subtracts. - * (the star) multiplies. Python does not use x for multiplication. - / divides, and always gives a float, even when the result is whole. - ** (two stars) raises to a power: 3 ** 2 is 3 times 3. ~~~python print(7 + 2) print(7 - 2) print(7 * 2) print(7 / 2) print(8 / 2) print(3 ** 2) ~~~ - Line 1: prints 9. - Line 2: prints 5. - Line 3: prints 14. - Line 4: prints 3.5. - Line 5: prints 4.0, not 4: the result of / is always a float. - Line 6: prints 9. ### Whole division // and remainder % Two operators work as a pair whenever you split something into whole groups: - // (floor division) divides and keeps only the whole part. 17 // 5 is 3, because 5 fits into 17 three whole times. - % (modulo) gives what is left over after that division. 17 % 5 is 2, because 3 times 5 is 15, and 17 minus 15 leaves 2. ~~~python eggs = 17 boxes = eggs // 6 left = eggs % 6 print(boxes, "full boxes and", left, "eggs left") ~~~ - Line 1: eggs holds 17. - Line 2: 6 fits into 17 two whole times, so boxes gets 2. - Line 3: 2 boxes use 12 eggs, so left gets 5. - Line 4: prints 2 full boxes and 5 eggs left. ### Converting units: minutes into hours Time works the same way. There are 60 minutes in an hour, so // 60 gives the whole hours and % 60 gives the minutes that do not make a full hour. ~~~python total_minutes = 200 hours = total_minutes // 60 minutes = total_minutes % 60 print(hours, minutes) ~~~ - Line 1: total_minutes holds 200. - Line 2: 60 fits into 200 three times, so hours gets 3. - Line 3: 3 hours are 180 minutes, so 20 are left: minutes gets 20. - Line 4: prints 3 20. ### Order of operations and parentheses Python follows the same priority rules as maths: ** first, then *, /, // and %, then + and -. Operators of the same priority run from left to right. Parentheses force a part to be calculated first. This matters when you chain operators: in a % b // c, Python does a % b first, then divides that result by c. ~~~python print(2 + 3 * 4) print((2 + 3) * 4) days_left = 100 % 30 // 7 print(days_left) ~~~ - Line 1: 3 * 4 goes first (12), then 2 is added: 14. - Line 2: the parentheses make 2 + 3 go first (5), then times 4: 20. - Line 3: left to right. 100 % 30 is 10 (100 days is 3 months of 30 days plus 10 days). Then 10 // 7 is 1 full week. days_left gets 1. - Line 4: prints 1. ### Rounding with round round(number, digits) rounds a number to the given number of decimal places. The two values inside the parentheses are separated by a comma. Values you hand to a function like this are called arguments. ~~~python price = 10 / 3 print(price) print(round(price, 2)) ~~~ - Line 1: price gets 3.3333333333333335 (computers store decimals with tiny imprecision). - Line 2: prints the long number. - Line 3: rounds to 2 decimals and prints 3.33. ### Common mistakes - Using / when you want a whole number. / gives a float such as 2.05. Use // for whole groups. - Mixing up // and %: // is "how many whole times", % is "what is left over". - Forgetting that the remainder must be taken from the original total before splitting it again into smaller units. - Writing x for multiplication. Use *. ### Recap - + - * / add, subtract, multiply and divide. / always gives a float. - ** is the power operator. - // gives the number of whole groups, % gives the leftover. - Same-priority operators run left to right. Parentheses go first. - round(x, 2) rounds to 2 decimal places.
py-strings: Real data is messy: names arrive with extra spaces, in the wrong case, or with first and last name stuck together. Python strings come with tools to clean and cut text, and to build new text from values. ### Methods: tools attached to a string A method is a function that belongs to a value. You call it with a dot after the value: text.upper(). The empty parentheses are still required. A string method never changes the original string. It gives you back a new string, which you usually store in a variable. - .strip() removes spaces at the start and the end (not in the middle). - .upper() makes every letter capital, .lower() makes every letter small. - .title() makes the first letter of each word capital and the rest small. ~~~python raw = " alan TURING " print("[" + raw.strip() + "]") print(raw.upper()) print(raw.lower()) print(raw.title()) print("[" + raw + "]") ~~~ - Line 1: raw holds the messy text, with two spaces on each side. - Line 2: + between strings glues them together. The brackets just make the edges visible: [alan TURING], the outer spaces are gone. - Line 3: prints ALAN TURING . - Line 4: prints alan turing . - Line 5: prints Alan Turing . - Line 6: prints [ alan TURING ]: raw itself never changed. ### Chaining methods Because each method returns a new string, you can call another method on the result straight away. Python works from left to right. ~~~python raw = " alan TURING " clean = raw.strip().title() print(clean) ~~~ - Line 1: the messy text. - Line 2: raw.strip() gives "alan TURING", then .title() on that gives "Alan Turing", which is stored in clean. - Line 3: prints Alan Turing. ### Indexing: one character at a time Each character in a string has a position number called an index. Counting starts at 0, not 1. You read one character with square brackets: word[0]. Negative numbers count from the end: -1 is the last character. A slice word[start:stop] takes several characters, from start up to but not including stop. len(word) gives the number of characters. ~~~python word = "Python" print(word[0]) print(word[1]) print(word[-1]) print(word[0:3]) print(len(word)) ~~~ - Line 1: positions are P=0, y=1, t=2, h=3, o=4, n=5. - Line 2: prints P. - Line 3: prints y. - Line 4: prints n, the last character. - Line 5: positions 0, 1 and 2: prints Pyt. - Line 6: prints 6. ### Splitting text into words .split() cuts a string at every run of spaces and gives back the pieces. The result is a list: several values in order, written inside square brackets. You will study lists later; for now, know that you read an item from a list with an index too, exactly like a character. And since each item is a string, you can index it again: parts[1][0] means "item 1, then its character 0". ~~~python city = "new york city" parts = city.split() print(parts) print(parts[1]) print(parts[1][0]) print(parts[0][0] + parts[2][0]) ~~~ - Line 1: one string with three words. - Line 2: parts gets the list ['new', 'york', 'city']. - Line 3: prints the list. - Line 4: item at index 1 is york. - Line 5: character 0 of york is y. - Line 6: n glued to c gives nc. ### f-strings: putting values inside text An f-string is a string with the letter f just before the opening quote. Inside it, anything in curly braces { } is replaced by its value. It is the easiest way to mix text and variables. ~~~python name = "Ada" age = 36 print(f"{name} is {age} years old") print(f"In 4 years: {age + 4}") print(f"[{name.upper()}]") ~~~ - Lines 1 and 2: two variables. - Line 3: {name} becomes Ada and {age} becomes 36: Ada is 36 years old. - Line 4: you can calculate inside the braces: prints In 4 years: 40. - Line 5: method calls work too, and characters outside the braces (here the brackets) are printed as they are: [ADA]. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting the f before the quote: the braces are then printed literally. - Forgetting the parentheses: raw.strip without () does not run the method. - Expecting raw.strip() alone to change raw. Store the result: clean = raw.strip(). - Counting from 1. The first character or item is at index 0. ### Recap - Methods are called with a dot: s.strip(), s.title(), s.upper(), s.lower(), s.split(). They return new values. - Methods can be chained, left to right. - s[0] is the first character, s[-1] the last, s[a:b] a slice, len(s) the length. - + glues strings together. - f"...{value}..." puts values inside text.
py-input: So far your programs always did the same thing. With input() a program can ask the person using it for information, like a name, a quantity or a price, and react to the answer. ### input reads one line input() waits for the user to type a line and press Enter, then gives back what was typed, as a string. You usually store it in a variable. On this page, the lines in the Input box are typed for you: the first input() receives the first line, the second input() receives the second line, and so on. ~~~python stdin=Ada name = input() print(f"Hello, {name}!") ~~~ - Line 1: input() reads the first input line, Ada, and stores the string "Ada" in name. - Line 2: prints Hello, Ada!. ### A prompt tells the user what to type You can put a string inside the parentheses. It is shown before the user types, as a question. It is called a prompt. It does not change the value that is read. ~~~python stdin=Lyon city = input("Which city? ") print("You chose", city) ~~~ - Line 1: shows Which city? , then reads Lyon into city. - Line 2: prints You chose Lyon. ### The trap: input always gives text Even when the user types digits, input() returns a string. And + between two strings does not add, it glues them together. ~~~python stdin=12|30 a = input() b = input() print(a + b) print(type(a)) ~~~ - Line 1: a gets the string "12". - Line 2: b gets the string "30". - Line 3: "12" + "30" glues the texts: prints 1230, not 42. - Line 4: prints <class 'str'>, the proof that a is text. ### Converting text into numbers int(text) turns a string of digits into a whole number. float(text) turns text like "2.5" into a decimal number. You can wrap the conversion directly around input(): Python runs the inner function first (read the line), then the outer one (convert it). ~~~python stdin=4|2.5 quantity = int(input("How many? ")) price = float(input("Unit price? ")) total = quantity * price print("Total:", total) ~~~ - Line 1: input reads "4", then int turns it into the number 4, stored in quantity. - Line 2: reads "2.5", and float turns it into 2.5, stored in price. - Line 3: now real maths works: total gets 10.0. - Line 4: prints Total: 10.0. ### Reading several values, one per line Each call to input() consumes exactly one line. To read a name and an age, call it twice. ~~~python stdin=Ada|36 name = input("Your name: ") age = int(input("Your age: ")) print(f"{name} will be {age + 1} next year") ~~~ - Line 1: reads the first line, Ada, into name. - Line 2: reads the second line, converts it, so age holds the number 36. - Line 3: age + 1 is 37: prints Ada will be 37 next year. Negative numbers work too: int("-5") gives -5. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting int(), so + glues text instead of adding. - Converting text that is not a number. int("abc") or int("2.5") stops the program with an error: ~~~text ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc' ~~~ - Calling input() once and expecting both lines. One call reads one line. - Mismatched parentheses in int(input()): every opening one needs a closing one. ### Recap - input() reads one line and always returns a string. An optional prompt goes inside the parentheses. - int(...) converts to a whole number, float(...) to a decimal. - int(input()) reads and converts in one step. - One input() call per line you want to read.
py-if: Programs constantly make choices: free shipping above a certain amount, a warning when stock is low, a different price for children. The if statement lets your program choose what to do based on a value. ### Comparisons give True or False A comparison checks two values and gives back a bool: True or False. Python has six comparison operators: - == equal to (two equals signs; one = is for assignment) - != not equal to - < less than, <= less than or equal to - > greater than, >= greater than or equal to ~~~python age = 17 print(age >= 18) print(age < 18) print(age == 17) print(age != 17) ~~~ - Line 1: age holds 17. - Line 2: is 17 greater than or equal to 18? No: prints False. - Line 3: is 17 less than 18? Yes: prints True. - Line 4: is 17 equal to 17? True. - Line 5: is 17 different from 17? False. ### if: run a block only when a condition is true You write if, then a condition, then a colon :. The lines that belong to the if come underneath, indented by 4 spaces. This indented group is called a block. Python runs the block only when the condition is True. The first line that is no longer indented is outside the block and always runs. ~~~python total = 65 if total >= 50: print("Free shipping!") print("Thanks for your order") print("Done") ~~~ - Line 1: total holds 65. - Line 2: the condition 65 >= 50 is True, so Python enters the block. - Lines 3 and 4: both indented, both run. - Line 5: not indented, so it runs whatever the condition was. Try changing 65 to 30: only Done is printed. ### else: the other case else: (with its colon, and no condition) gives a block to run when the if condition is False. Exactly one of the two blocks runs. ~~~python stock = 3 if stock > 0: print("In stock") else: print("Sold out") ~~~ - Line 1: stock holds 3. - Line 2: 3 > 0 is True. - Line 3: runs, prints In stock. - Lines 4 and 5: skipped, because the if branch already ran. ### elif: a chain of choices elif means "else if". It adds another condition to check when the previous ones were false. Python checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first one that is true, then skips the rest of the chain. The final else catches everything left over. Because of this, the order matters: put the strictest test first. ~~~python stdin=12 age = int(input()) if age >= 65: print("Senior ticket") elif age >= 18: print("Adult ticket") elif age >= 4: print("Child ticket") else: print("Free") ~~~ - Line 1: reads 12 and stores the number in age. - Line 2: 12 >= 65 is false, so its block is skipped. - Line 4: 12 >= 18 is false, skipped. - Line 6: 12 >= 4 is true: line 7 prints Child ticket. - Lines 8 and 9: skipped, because a branch already ran. If the order were reversed (age >= 4 first), a 70 year old would get a child ticket, since 70 is also greater than 4. ### and, or, not You can combine conditions. and is true only when both sides are true. or is true when at least one side is true. not flips True into False and back. ~~~python temp = 22 raining = False if temp > 18 and not raining: print("Picnic time") if temp < 0 or raining: print("Stay inside") ~~~ - Lines 1 and 2: two variables. - Line 3: temp > 18 is true, not raining is not False, which is true. Both are true, so line 4 prints Picnic time. - Line 5: temp < 0 is false and raining is false, so the or is false and line 6 does not run. ### Common mistakes - Writing = instead of == in a condition, which is a SyntaxError. - Forgetting the colon at the end of if, elif or else. - Wrong indentation: the block must be indented, and all its lines by the same amount. - Checking thresholds in the wrong order, so a lower test catches values meant for a higher one. ### Recap - Comparisons (== != < <= > >=) give True or False. - if condition: then an indented block. - elif adds more tests, else catches the rest. Only the first true branch runs. - and, or, not combine conditions.
py-for: Computers are great at repeating work: sending the same email to every customer, adding up every sale, printing every line of a report. A for loop repeats a block of code once for each item in a collection. ### Looping over a list of items A list is several values in square brackets, separated by commas, like ["apple", "kiwi", "pear"]. (Lists get their own lesson later.) The loop is written for name in collection:. The word in means "taking each item from". On each round, called an iteration, Python puts the next item into the loop variable and runs the indented block. ~~~python for fruit in ["apple", "kiwi", "pear"]: print("I like", fruit) print("End of the list") ~~~ - Line 1, round 1: fruit gets "apple". - Line 2: prints I like apple. Back to line 1. - Round 2: fruit gets "kiwi", line 2 prints I like kiwi. - Round 3: fruit gets "pear", line 2 prints I like pear. - Line 3: no items left, the loop ends. This line is not indented, so it runs once: End of the list. Use the Step through button to watch fruit change on each round. ### Looping over a string A string is also a collection: of characters. A for loop over it gives one character per round. ~~~python for letter in "Hey": print(letter) ~~~ - Round 1: letter is "H", printed. - Round 2: letter is "e", printed. - Round 3: letter is "y", printed. ### range: counting numbers Often you just want to repeat with numbers. range(stop) produces the whole numbers from 0 up to, but not including, stop. So range(3) gives 0, 1, 2: three numbers. ~~~python for i in range(3): print("Round", i) ~~~ - Round 1: i is 0, prints Round 0. - Round 2: i is 1, prints Round 1. - Round 3: i is 2, prints Round 2. The number 3 itself is never reached. ### range with a start and a step range(start, stop) starts at start instead of 0, and still stops just before stop. A third value, the step, sets how much to add each time: range(start, stop, step). To count from 1 to 5 included, write range(1, 6). ~~~python for day in range(1, 6): print(f"Day {day} of 5") for n in range(0, 20, 5): print(n) ~~~ - Line 1: day takes the values 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 (6 is excluded). - Line 2: on each round the f-string puts the current day in the text: Day 1 of 5, then Day 2 of 5, and so on. - Line 3: n starts at 0 and goes up by 5 each round: 0, 5, 10, 15. 20 is excluded. - Line 4: prints each value. ### Using the loop variable in a calculation The loop variable is an ordinary variable: you can do maths with it, and combine it with other variables, for example a number read with input(). ~~~python stdin=4 size = int(input()) for i in range(1, 4): print(f"{i} box(es) of {size} = {i * size} items") ~~~ - Line 1: reads 4 into size. - Line 2: i will take the values 1, 2 and 3. - Line 3, round 1: i * size is 4: prints 1 box(es) of 4 = 4 items. - Round 2: 2 box(es) of 4 = 8 items. Round 3: 3 box(es) of 4 = 12 items. ### Keeping a running total A common pattern: create a variable before the loop, then update it inside the loop. Writing total = total + n means "take the current total, add n, store the result back in total". ~~~python total = 0 for n in range(1, 5): total = total + n print("after adding", n, "total is", total) print("Final:", total) ~~~ - Line 1: total starts at 0. - Lines 2 to 4: n is 1, so total becomes 1. Then n is 2, total becomes 3. Then 3, total 6. Then 4, total 10. - Line 5: after the loop, prints Final: 10. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting the colon at the end of the for line. - Forgetting to indent the lines that should repeat, or indenting a line that should run only once. - Off by one: range(1, 10) stops at 9. To include 10, write range(1, 11). - Putting the starting value of a running total inside the loop, which resets it on every round. ### Recap - for item in collection: runs the indented block once per item. - Lists and strings can be looped over directly. - range(stop), range(start, stop), range(start, stop, step) produce numbers, never including stop. - The loop variable can be used in f-strings and calculations.
py-while: A for loop is perfect when you know what to go through. A while loop is for when you repeat until something happens: keep asking until the answer is valid, keep retrying until it works, keep counting until a limit. ### while: repeat as long as a condition is true You write while, a condition and a colon, then an indented block. Before each round Python checks the condition. If it is True, the block runs and Python goes back to check again. As soon as it is False, the loop ends and the program continues after it. ~~~python count = 3 while count > 0: print(count) count = count - 1 print("Lift off") ~~~ - Line 1: count holds 3. - Line 2: 3 > 0 is true, enter the block. - Line 3: prints 3. - Line 4: count becomes 2. Back to line 2. - The same happens with 2, then 1. After printing 1, count becomes 0. - Line 2 again: 0 > 0 is false, the loop ends. - Line 5: prints Lift off. Something inside the loop must change the condition. If count never went down, the loop would never end. This is called an infinite loop; this page stops it after 3 seconds. ### Shortcuts: += and -= Updating a variable from its own value is so common that Python has short forms. i += 1 means exactly i = i + 1, and count -= 1 means count = count - 1. ~~~python i = 1 while i <= 5: print("Item", i) i += 1 print("i ended at", i) ~~~ - Line 1: i starts at 1. - Lines 2 to 4: while i is at most 5, print it and add 1. i goes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. - After printing Item 5, i becomes 6 and 6 <= 5 is false. - Line 5: prints i ended at 6. ### Testing "is a multiple of" with % You met %, the remainder. A number is a multiple of 3 exactly when dividing it by 3 leaves nothing: n % 3 == 0. This is how you test divisibility. ~~~python n = 1 while n <= 6: if n % 2 == 0: print(n, "is even") else: print(n, "is odd") n += 1 ~~~ - Line 1: n starts at 1. - Line 3, round 1: 1 % 2 is 1, not 0, so the else prints 1 is odd. - Round 2: 2 % 2 is 0, so it prints 2 is even. - And so on up to 6. Line 7 moves n forward on every round, whichever branch ran. ### Checking the combined case first When a number can match two rules, check the combined rule first. Remember that an if / elif chain runs only the first true branch. A number that is a multiple of both 2 and 3 is a multiple of 6. ~~~python n = 1 while n <= 7: if n % 6 == 0: print(n, "both") elif n % 2 == 0: print(n, "two") elif n % 3 == 0: print(n, "three") else: print(n) n += 1 ~~~ - Rounds 1 to 5: 1 prints 1, 2 prints 2 two, 3 prints 3 three, 4 prints 4 two, 5 prints 5. - Round 6: 6 % 6 == 0 is true, prints 6 both, and the other tests are skipped. - Round 7: prints 7. Then n becomes 8 and the loop ends. If the n % 2 test came first, 6 would print 6 two and never reach the combined test. ### break and continue Two keywords control a loop from inside. break leaves the loop immediately. continue skips the rest of the current round and goes back to the condition check. In a while loop, make sure the counter moves forward before a continue, otherwise the same value is tested forever. ~~~python n = 0 while n < 10: n += 1 if n % 2 == 0: continue if n > 7: break print(n) print("stopped at", n) ~~~ - Line 3: n goes up at the start of each round, before any continue. - Line 4: for even numbers, continue jumps straight back to line 2, so they are never printed. - Line 6: when n reaches 9 (the first odd number above 7), break ends the loop. - Line 8: prints 1, 3, 5 and 7. - Line 9: prints stopped at 9. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting to update the counter, which makes an infinite loop. - Using continue before the counter update in a while loop: the counter never moves. - Putting the update inside an if or else block, so it only happens in some rounds. - Testing a single rule before the combined rule in an elif chain. ### Recap - while condition: repeats its block as long as the condition is true. - Something in the block must eventually make the condition false. - i += 1 is short for i = i + 1. - n % k == 0 means "n is a multiple of k". - break leaves the loop, continue jumps to the next round.
py-lists: A list keeps many values together, in order, under one name: all the prices of an order, all the temperatures of a week, all the names in a team. You can add to it, remove from it and ask it questions like "what is the biggest value?". ### Creating a list and reading items You write a list with square brackets, the items separated by commas. Each item has an index starting at 0, just like the characters of a string. len(list) gives the number of items. ~~~python prices = [12, 5, 30, 8] print(prices) print(prices[0]) print(prices[-1]) print(len(prices)) ~~~ - Line 1: prices holds a list of 4 numbers. - Line 2: prints the whole list: [12, 5, 30, 8]. - Line 3: index 0 is the first item: 12. - Line 4: index -1 is the last item: 8. - Line 5: 4 items, so 4. ### Changing a list Unlike a string, a list can be changed in place. These methods change the list itself: - .append(x) adds x at the end. - .insert(i, x) puts x at position i, moving the others right. - .remove(x) deletes the first item equal to x. - .pop() removes the last item and gives it back to you. ~~~python team = ["Ada", "Linus"] team.append("Grace") print(team) team.insert(0, "Guido") print(team) team.remove("Linus") print(team) last = team.pop() print(last, team) ~~~ - Line 1: team holds 2 names. - Line 2: team becomes ['Ada', 'Linus', 'Grace']. Line 3 prints it. - Line 4: "Guido" goes to position 0: ['Guido', 'Ada', 'Linus', 'Grace']. - Line 6: "Linus" is removed: ['Guido', 'Ada', 'Grace']. - Line 8: the last item, "Grace", is taken out and stored in last. - Line 9: prints Grace ['Guido', 'Ada']. ### Asking questions about a list These functions take a list and give back an answer without changing the list: - sum(list) adds all the numbers. - max(list) and min(list) give the biggest and the smallest. - sorted(list) gives a new list in increasing order. sorted(list, reverse=True) gives decreasing order. The reverse=True part is a named argument: an option given by name. - x in list gives True if x is one of the items. ~~~python prices = [12, 5, 30, 8] print(sum(prices)) print(max(prices), min(prices)) print(sorted(prices)) print(sorted(prices, reverse=True)) print(30 in prices, 99 in prices) print(prices) ~~~ - Line 2: 12 + 5 + 30 + 8: prints 55. - Line 3: prints 30 5. - Line 4: prints [5, 8, 12, 30]. - Line 5: prints [30, 12, 8, 5]. - Line 6: prints True False. - Line 7: the original list is unchanged: [12, 5, 30, 8]. ### The average An average is the total divided by how many values there are: sum(list) / len(list). The division gives a float, often with many decimals, so wrap it in round(..., 1) to keep one decimal. Python computes the innermost parentheses first. ~~~python scores = [14, 9, 17, 12] average = sum(scores) / len(scores) print(average) print(round(average, 1)) print(round(sum([3, 4, 4]) / 3, 1)) ~~~ - Line 2: sum(scores) is 52, len(scores) is 4, so average gets 13.0. - Line 3: prints 13.0. - Line 4: prints 13.0 again, already one decimal. - Line 5: everything in one line: 11 divided by 3 is 3.666..., rounded to 3.7. ### Building a new list with a loop To keep only some items, start with an empty list [], loop over the original list, and .append the items that pass an if test. The new list keeps the original order. ~~~python prices = [12, 5, 30, 8] cheap = [] for p in prices: if p < 10: cheap.append(p) print("checked", p, "cheap is now", cheap) print(cheap) ~~~ - Line 2: cheap starts empty. - Round 1: p is 12, not below 10, nothing added. - Round 2: p is 5, so cheap becomes [5]. - Round 3: 30 is skipped. Round 4: 8 is added: [5, 8]. - Line 6 shows the list after each round. Line 7 prints [5, 8]. ### Common mistakes - Writing cheap = cheap.append(p). append changes the list and returns nothing, so this replaces your list with None. Just write cheap.append(p). - Creating the empty list inside the loop, which empties it on every round. - Confusing "strictly above" (>) with "above or equal" (>=). - Forgetting round when a specific number of decimals is asked. ### Recap - [a, b, c] makes a list. lst[0] is the first item, lst[-1] the last. - append, insert, remove, pop change the list. - len, sum, max, min, sorted and in answer questions. - Average: round(sum(lst) / len(lst), 1). - Filter by looping and appending to a new empty list.
py-dicts: A dictionary stores pairs: a key and its value. Think of a phone book (name to number) or a price list (product to price). You look things up by key instead of by position, and it is instant. ### Creating a dictionary and looking up a key A dictionary, or dict, is written with curly braces { }. Inside, each pair is key: value, and pairs are separated by commas. To read a value, put its key in square brackets. ~~~python prices = {"coffee": 2.5, "tea": 2.0, "cake": 4.0} print(prices) print(prices["tea"]) print(len(prices)) ~~~ - Line 1: prices holds 3 pairs. "coffee" is a key, 2.5 is its value. - Line 2: prints the whole dict. - Line 3: looks up the key "tea" and prints 2.0. - Line 4: len counts pairs: 3. ### Adding and updating Assigning to a key adds the pair if the key is new, or replaces the value if the key already exists. A dict never holds the same key twice. ~~~python stock = {"apple": 5} stock["pear"] = 3 stock["apple"] = 10 stock["apple"] = stock["apple"] + 1 print(stock) ~~~ - Line 1: stock holds one pair. - Line 2: "pear" is new, so it is added with the value 3. - Line 3: "apple" exists, so its value is replaced by 10. - Line 4: reads the current value (10), adds 1, stores 11. - Line 5: prints {'apple': 11, 'pear': 3}. ### Missing keys: in and .get Reading a key that does not exist with square brackets stops the program with a KeyError. Two safe tools: key in d tells you if the key exists, and d.get(key, default) gives the value, or the default when the key is missing. ~~~python stock = {"apple": 5} print("apple" in stock, "kiwi" in stock) print(stock.get("apple", 0)) print(stock.get("kiwi", 0)) ~~~ - Line 2: prints True False. - Line 3: the key exists, so .get returns its value: 5. - Line 4: "kiwi" is missing, so .get returns the default: 0. ### Looping over a dict A for loop over a dict gives you its keys. .items() gives the pairs, and you can receive each pair into two loop variables at once: for key, value in d.items():. ~~~python prices = {"coffee": 2.5, "tea": 2.0} for product in prices: print(product) for product, price in prices.items(): print(f"{product} costs {price}") ~~~ - Lines 2 and 3: product gets "coffee", then "tea". - Line 4: on round 1, product is "coffee" and price is 2.5. - Line 5: prints coffee costs 2.5, then tea costs 2.0. ### Counting things The classic use of a dict is counting. Start with an empty dict {}. For each item, take its current count with .get(item, 0) (0 the first time you see it), add 1, and store it back. ~~~python counts = {} for color in ["red", "blue", "red", "green", "red"]: counts[color] = counts.get(color, 0) + 1 print(color, counts) ~~~ - Round 1: "red" is missing, .get gives 0, so counts["red"] becomes 1. - Round 2: "blue" becomes 1. - Round 3: "red" exists with 1, so it becomes 2. - Rounds 4 and 5: "green" becomes 1, then "red" becomes 3. - Line 4 shows the dict growing: it ends as {'red': 3, 'blue': 1, 'green': 1}. To count words in a sentence, loop over sentence.split() instead of a list. ### Finding the key with the biggest value max(d) alone compares the keys themselves (alphabetically for text). The named argument key= tells max what to compare instead. With key=d.get, it compares d.get(k) for each key k, which is the value, and still returns the key. Note: d.get has no parentheses here, because you hand over the method itself for max to call. ~~~python counts = {"red": 3, "blue": 1, "green": 1} print(max(counts)) best = max(counts, key=counts.get) print(best) ~~~ - Line 2: compares the keys as text: red is last alphabetically, so it prints red (correct here only by luck). - Line 3: compares the values 3, 1 and 1, and returns the key of the biggest: best gets "red". - Line 4: prints red. ### Common mistakes - Reading a missing key with d[key], which raises a KeyError. Use d.get(key, 0). - Writing key=counts.get() with parentheses inside max. - Using max(counts) without key=, which compares keys, not counts. ### Recap - {"key": value} makes a dict. d[key] reads, d[key] = v adds or updates. - key in d and d.get(key, default) handle missing keys safely. - for k, v in d.items(): loops over pairs. - Counting: counts[x] = counts.get(x, 0) + 1. - max(d, key=d.get) gives the key with the largest value.
py-sets: Two more ways to group values. A tuple is a fixed record that cannot change, like a GPS position. A set keeps each value only once, which is perfect for removing duplicates, like the same email address entered twice. ### Tuples: fixed groups of values A tuple is written with round brackets, the items separated by commas. You read items by index like a list, but you cannot add, remove or replace anything. Use it for values that belong together and should not change. ~~~python point = (3, 4) print(point) print(point[0], point[1]) print(len(point)) ~~~ - Line 1: point holds a tuple of two numbers. - Line 2: prints (3, 4). - Line 3: index 0 is 3, index 1 is 4. - Line 4: prints 2. ### Unpacking You can put each item of a tuple (or a list) into its own variable in one line. The number of names on the left must match the number of items. This is what for k, v in d.items() was already doing. ~~~python point = (3, 4) x, y = point print("x is", x, "and y is", y) user, domain = "ana@gmail.com".split("@") print(user, domain) ~~~ - Line 2: x gets 3 and y gets 4. - Line 3: prints x is 3 and y is 4. - Line 4: .split("@") cuts the text at the @ character instead of at spaces, giving the list ['ana', 'gmail.com']. user gets "ana", domain gets "gmail.com". - Line 5: prints ana gmail.com. Without unpacking you could write "ana@gmail.com".split("@")[1] to get the part after the @ directly. ### Sets: unique values A set is written with curly braces, like a dict but with single values instead of pairs. A set keeps each value only once and has no order, so it has no index. set(a_list) turns a list into a set, removing duplicates. An empty set is written set(), because {} means an empty dict. ~~~python numbers = [3, 1, 3, 2, 1, 3] unique = set(numbers) print(unique) print(len(numbers), len(unique)) print(2 in unique) ~~~ - Line 1: a list with duplicates. - Line 2: unique gets {1, 2, 3}: each value once. - Line 3: prints the set. For text values the printed order can vary from one run to another, since sets have no order. - Line 4: prints 6 3: six items in the list, three distinct. - Line 5: in works on sets and is very fast: True. ### Adding to a set, and sorting it .add(x) puts a value into a set. Adding a value that is already there does nothing. To get the values in a reliable order, sorted(a_set) returns a new list, sorted alphabetically for text. ~~~python cities = set() for c in ["Paris", "Lyon", "Paris", "Nice"]: cities.add(c) print(len(cities), "distinct so far") result = sorted(cities) print(result) print(type(result)) ~~~ - Line 1: cities starts as an empty set. - Rounds 1 and 2: "Paris", then "Lyon" are added: 1, then 2 distinct. - Round 3: "Paris" is already there, so the count stays 2. - Round 4: "Nice" is added: 3. - Line 5: result gets ['Lyon', 'Nice', 'Paris']. - Line 7: prints <class 'list'>: sorted always gives a list. ### Combining sets Sets can be combined with operators: | (union) gives everything in either set, & (intersection) gives what is in both, - (difference) gives what is in the first but not the second. ~~~python a = {1, 2, 3} b = {2, 3, 4} print(a | b) print(a & b) print(a - b) ~~~ - Line 3: prints {1, 2, 3, 4}. - Line 4: prints {2, 3}. - Line 5: prints {1}. ### Common mistakes - Writing {} for an empty set: that creates an empty dict. Use set(). - Trying my_set[0]: sets have no positions. - Expecting a set to print in a fixed order. Use sorted() when the order matters. - Using .append on a set. Sets use .add. ### Recap - (a, b) is a tuple: fixed, indexable. x, y = pair unpacks it. - text.split("@") cuts at a chosen character. - set(lst) removes duplicates. .add adds, in checks. - sorted(a_set) gives a sorted list. - |, &, - combine sets.
py-comp: You often build a new collection from an old one: the prices with tax, only the paid orders, a name for each id. A comprehension does that in one readable line, instead of the empty-list, loop and append pattern. ### From a loop to a list comprehension Here is the pattern you know, and the same result as a comprehension. A list comprehension is written in square brackets: first the expression that makes each new item, then a for part saying where the items come from. ~~~python doubled = [] for n in [1, 2, 3]: doubled.append(n * 2) print(doubled) doubled2 = [n * 2 for n in [1, 2, 3]] print(doubled2) ~~~ - Lines 1 to 3: the classic way. doubled becomes [2, 4, 6]. - Line 4: prints [2, 4, 6]. - Line 6: read it as "n * 2, for each n in the list". Python loops for you and collects every result into a new list. - Line 7: prints the same [2, 4, 6]. ### Using range and list() Comprehensions work with any collection, including range. list(range(1, 6)) turns a range into a real list, which is handy to see its content. ~~~python nums = list(range(1, 6)) print(nums) squares = [n * n for n in nums] print(squares) ~~~ - Line 1: nums gets [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. - Line 3: n * n for each n: squares gets [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]. ### Adding a filter with if You can put an if at the end. Only the items for which the condition is true are used. Read it as "expression, for each item, if condition". ~~~python nums = list(range(1, 11)) small = [n for n in nums if n < 4] odds = [n for n in nums if n % 2 == 1] tens = [n * 10 for n in nums if n % 3 == 0] print(small) print(odds) print(tens) ~~~ - Line 2: keeps n unchanged, only when n < 4: [1, 2, 3]. - Line 3: n % 2 == 1 is true for odd numbers: [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]. - Line 4: first filters the multiples of 3 (3, 6, 9), then applies n * 10 to each: [30, 60, 90]. - Lines 5 to 7: print the three lists. The filter is tested first, then the expression is computed for the items that passed. ### Set comprehensions The same thing in curly braces gives a set, so duplicates disappear. ~~~python words = ["Hi", "hi", "HEY", "hey"] lowered = {w.lower() for w in words} print(sorted(lowered)) ~~~ - Line 2: w.lower() for each word gives "hi", "hi", "hey", "hey". The set keeps each once. - Line 3: sorted gives a list in a fixed order: ['hey', 'hi']. ### Dict comprehensions With curly braces and a key: value expression, you get a dict. Each item from the loop produces one pair. ~~~python prices = [10, 25, 40] with_tax = {p: p * 1.2 for p in prices} print(with_tax) cities = ["Paris", "Nice"] first_letter = {c: c[0] for c in cities} print(first_letter) ~~~ - Line 2: for each p, the key is p and the value is p * 1.2. - Line 3: prints {10: 12.0, 25: 30.0, 40: 48.0}. - Line 5: the key is the city, the value is its first character. - Line 6: prints {'Paris': 'P', 'Nice': 'N'}. Any function can be used in the value part, for example len(c) to get the number of characters. ### Common mistakes - Putting the if before the for: [n if n > 2 for n in nums] is a SyntaxError. The filter goes at the end. - Forgetting the colon in a dict comprehension: {c, len(c) for c in cities} is not valid. - Using square brackets when a dict is wanted: square brackets always build a list. - Writing n % 2 when you mean even numbers: that is true for odd ones. Even is n % 2 == 0. ### Recap - [expr for x in items] builds a list. - [expr for x in items if condition] keeps only the items that pass. - {expr for x in items} builds a set. - {key: value for x in items} builds a dict. - list(range(a, b)) turns a range into a list.
